items.body_md:
On August 21, Judge Eumi K. Lee entered an order — Dkt. 477 — resolving both an administrative motion and the pending motion to intervene filed by Cengage Learning and Hachette Book Group (Dkt. 342), formally closing the publisher-intervention track in *In re Google Generative AI Copyright Litigation*, 5:23-cv-03440. The companion administrative motion, Dkt. 478, filed the same day under Civil Local Rule 7-11, relates to that same intervention cluster. The order follows Cengage and Hachette's July 10 administrative motion to withdraw their intervention bid (Dkt. 473), which itself was contested — Google opposed it on July 14 (Dkt. 474) and the publishers sought leave to reply on July 15 (Dkt. 475). The August 21 order resolves that contested withdrawal proceeding.

The procedural endgame here tracks a strategic pivot that matters for recovery posture. 
With the new lawsuit, Cengage and Hachette withdrew their motion to take part in the 2023 suit, observing that Google could assert that a three-year statute of limitations pertains to the class member claims.
 That limitations concern, combined with the pendency of class certification in this case without a ruling on the intervention, drove the publishers to file a standalone action rather than remain tethered to a class whose scope and adequacy of representation they could not control. 
On July 13, 2026, Hachette Book Group, Cengage Learning, Elsevier, and author Scott Turow filed a putative class action lawsuit against Google for willful infringement of millions of textual works to develop Google's Gemini large language models.
 
The proposed class action, filed July 10 in federal court in New York, accuses Google of illegally copying millions of works to train Gemini, including works scraped from "behind paywalls," from "known pirate sources," and books scanned and submitted via Google Books, Google Play, and Google Scholar.
 
The AAP stated the decision to file its own suit "aims to preserve the right to pursue all the claims that publishers and their authors have against Google, including important ones that fall outside the putative class in that case."


For claimants in the 5:23-cv-03440 class, the departure of Cengage and Hachette as proposed intervenors removes a potential source of publisher-side representation in the class certification calculus and eliminates the intra-class tension Google had been exploiting. 
Despite holding a hearing nearly five months ago on class certification, Judge Lee has yet to rule on the publishers' motion to intervene in the case
 — a delay that contributed to the publishers' decision to exit. The outstanding class certification ruling now becomes the next substantive milestone in this proceeding: that order will define the plaintiff class's composition and, directly, the universe of claimants able to share in any eventual recovery. No hearing date for the class certification ruling has been separately docketed; the next concrete date to watch is whenever Judge Lee issues that order.

items.body_md:
On August 13, the docket recorded a Notice of Appearance/Substitution/Change/Withdrawal of Attorney — procedural and routine, with no bearing on claim exposure or case trajectory.

The substantive posture entering today remains fixed on the unresolved motion sequence in the consolidated N.D. California action (5:23-cv-03440, Judge Lee). The most recent contested activity was the July 10–15 Cengage/Hachette motion to withdraw their intervention (Dkt. 473), Google's opposition (Dkt. 474), and the movants' administrative motion for leave to reply (Dkt. 475, with responses due July 20). That withdrawal, if granted, would remove the publisher intervenors from the consolidated track — a notable posture shift given that those same parties filed a separate, stand-alone action in the Southern District of New York on July 10 (
*Hachette Book Group et al. v. Google LLC*, No. 1:26-cv-05870, S.D.N.Y., with the complaint docketed July 10
). The two-track strategy — exit the intervention, press a direct action — concentrates the publishers' claims in a forum and on pleadings they fully control, rather than subordinating them to the consolidated class posture in California.

The New York complaint's theory is not procedurally identical to what was pending in the consolidated action. 
Hachette, Elsevier, Cengage, and Scott Turow allege Google used millions of copyrighted books and journal articles without permission to build Gemini, copying works from sources including Google Books, online libraries, and allegedly pirated websites
. 
The complaint separately alleges Google intentionally removed or changed copyright information to "conceal… that its Gemini Models were trained on stolen materials,"
 adding a DMCA § 1202 CMI-removal layer on top of the core infringement theory. 
The suit also argues Gemini now competes directly with the books it learned from by generating content that could reduce demand for the original materials
 — the § 107(4) market-harm prong that will be the decisive fair-use battleground across the AI-copyright track. The next concrete milestone in the N.D. California action is the outcome of the Dkt. 473/474/475 withdrawal motion sequence; once Judge Lee rules, the intervention question is resolved and the class certification record (indexed at Dkt. 472) governs the remaining plaintiff structure in the consolidated case.
